description: The nervous system's divisions — CNS, PNS, somatic, autonomic — and fight or flight.
content_html:
The Human Nervous System

Every thought, movement and bodily function depends on your nervous system. Psychologists study this system because it underlies all behaviour — from blinking to solving a maths problem. The nervous system has two main divisions: the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS).

Key Fact

The nervous system divides into CNS (brain + spinal cord) and PNS (all other nerves). The PNS divides further into the somatic nervous system and the autonomic nervous system.

Divisions of the Peripheral Nervous System

The PNS has two branches. The somatic nervous system handles voluntary movements and sends sensory signals from the skin, eyes and ears back to the brain. When you decide to raise your hand in class, the somatic system carries that instruction to your arm muscles.

The autonomic nervous system (ANS) works without conscious thought. It regulates heart rate, digestion, breathing and gland activity. The ANS is divided into two opposing branches: the sympathetic branch, which activates the body in times of stress, and the parasympathetic branch, which returns the body to a calm resting state.

When the sympathetic branch activates, it causes the heart to beat faster, breathing to quicken, the pupils to dilate, digestion to slow, and adrenaline to be released into the bloodstream. These changes prepare the body for intense physical action.

Once the threat passes, the parasympathetic branch takes over. It slows the heart rate, narrows the pupils, resumes digestion and calms breathing. Think of sympathetic as the “accelerator” and parasympathetic as the “brake.”

The Fight or Flight Response

When the brain detects a threat — real or perceived — the sympathetic branch of the ANS triggers the fight or flight response. The hypothalamus signals the adrenal glands to release adrenaline. This hormone causes a rapid cascade of physical changes: the heart rate increases, blood is redirected to the muscles, glucose is released for energy, and non-essential systems such as digestion are suppressed.

These changes evolved because they gave our ancestors a survival advantage when confronted by predators. Today, the same response can be triggered by modern threats such as a difficult exam or a confrontation, even though physical “fighting” or “fleeing” is rarely needed.

Key Fact

The fight or flight response is triggered by the sympathetic ANS, which releases adrenaline from the adrenal glands. Key effects include increased heart rate, redirected blood flow to muscles, release of glucose, and suppression of digestion.

The James–Lange Theory of Emotion

Most people assume emotions cause bodily reactions — you feel afraid, and then your heart races. The James–Lange theory of emotion reverses this: it argues that the body reacts first, and the emotion is what we experience when the brain interprets those bodily changes. In other words, you run and then feel afraid, rather than feeling afraid and then running.

William James and Carl Lange proposed this idea independently in 1884. Their shared conclusion was that without the physical response, there would be no emotional experience. If your heart did not race, you would not feel fear — you would simply observe a threat without any feeling attached.

A strength of the James–Lange theory is that it provides a testable, physiological account of emotion that links psychology to biology. It aligns with research showing that people with spinal cord injuries, who cannot feel their bodily responses, often report reduced emotional intensity — supporting the idea that physical feedback matters.

However, a weakness is that many emotions produce similar bodily states. Fear and excitement, for example, both involve increased heart rate and adrenaline. If emotions were simply the interpretation of bodily changes, it would be hard to explain how we distinguish between them. The theory also does not fully account for the role of cognition — our thoughts and memories — in shaping emotional experience.

Why the Nervous System Matters for Psychology

Understanding the nervous system helps explain why stress can be harmful over time. The fight or flight response is designed for short bursts of danger, not prolonged worry. Chronic stress keeps the sympathetic ANS activated, raising blood pressure and suppressing the immune system. This is why psychological wellbeing and physical health are closely linked — a core insight of modern health psychology.
exam_tip_html: On “describe” or “explain” questions about the fight or flight response, name the branch of the ANS involved (sympathetic), the hormone released (adrenaline), and at least two specific physical changes. For the James–Lange theory, always state the direction of causation: bodily change first, then emotional interpretation — this is the part students most often reverse.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The nervous system divides into CNS (brain and spinal cord) and PNS (all other nerves). The PNS branches into the somatic system (voluntary) and the autonomic system (involuntary), which is itself split into sympathetic (activating) and parasympathetic (calming).
  • The fight or flight response is triggered by the sympathetic ANS via adrenaline release, causing increased heart rate, muscle blood flow and glucose, with digestion suppressed.
  • The James–Lange theory proposes that emotions are the brain’s interpretation of bodily changes, not their cause — so the physical reaction comes first.

practice_questions.text:
Which part of the nervous system controls the fight or flight response?
A) The central nervous system
B) The somatic nervous system
C) The sympathetic autonomic nervous system
D) The parasympathetic autonomic nervous system
practice_questions.marks: C) The sympathetic autonomic nervous system [1 mark]

Mastering: A precise definition stating it is the division of the PNS that controls involuntary bodily functions such as heart rate, digestion or breathing — both the involuntary nature and a specific function stated [2 marks].
Secure: Correct core idea — involuntary control — with vague or missing example [1 mark].
Developing: Partial answer identifying automatic processes without linking to the PNS [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to the body during the fight or flight response.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per accurate, distinct point up to 3 marks. Students may include: the sympathetic ANS is activated; adrenaline is released by the adrenal glands; heart rate increases; blood is redirected to the muscles; glucose is released for energy; digestion slows or stops; pupils dilate; breathing quickens.
Mastering: Three distinct, accurate physiological changes named with a brief explanation of why each occurs.
Secure: Three changes named with limited explanation.
Developing: Two changes named.
Emerging: One change named or vague description only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the James–Lange theory of emotion. In your answer, refer to the relationship between bodily changes and emotional experience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear statement that bodily changes precede and cause emotions (not the other way around), with an accurate example (e.g. heart races → we interpret this as fear) and a link to the role of the brain interpreting physical feedback. Two developed points.
Secure: Correct direction of causation stated and an example given; some explanation of the theory's logic.
Developing: Partially correct — may state correct direction but without explanation; or reversal of direction.
Emerging: Vague mention of the theory without accurate content.

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure and function of the human nervous system, including its main divisions.
practice_questions.marks:
This question asks students to describe the nervous system rather than a named study. Award marks for: CNS described as brain + spinal cord (1); PNS described as all nerves outside the CNS (1); somatic nervous system identified as controlling voluntary movement and sensory input (1); autonomic nervous system identified as controlling involuntary functions (1); sympathetic and parasympathetic branches distinguished in terms of function (1).
Mastering: All five elements accurately described with clear function for each division.
Secure: Four elements described.
Developing: Two or three divisions named with basic functions.
Emerging: Only CNS/PNS named without function.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the James–Lange theory of emotion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of the theory (bodily changes → brain interpretation → emotion; not emotion → body); at least two specific physical examples; two elaborated evaluation points (e.g. similar bodily states for different emotions as a weakness; spinal cord injury research as a strength), with each evaluation point developed with a reason.
Secure: Accurate description of direction of causation; two evaluation points with some development.
Developing: Partially correct description; one evaluation point with reasoning, or two without.
Emerging: Some relevant content but description is vague or direction reversed; evaluation is a single unsupported point.
[Description AO1 ~4 marks; Evaluation AO3 ~5 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which division of the nervous system controls voluntary skeletal muscle movements?
According to the James–Lange theory, what comes first in the sequence that produces an emotion?
options: The conscious feeling of the emotion
A decision made in the prefrontal cortex
A physical change in the body

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ nervous system controls involuntary bodily functions such as heart rate and digestion.
During the fight or flight response, the adrenal glands release the hormone _____.
Match each nervous system division to its correct description.
right: Regulates involuntary functions such as heart rate

flashcard_questions.q: What two structures make up the central nervous system?
flashcard_questions.a: The brain and the spinal cord.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the somatic nervous system responsible for?
flashcard_questions.a: Voluntary movements and relaying sensory information to the CNS.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of functions does the autonomic nervous system control — voluntary or involuntary?
flashcard_questions.a: Involuntary functions — it operates without conscious thought.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a bodily process controlled by the autonomic nervous system.
flashcard_questions.a: Heart rate (also accept: digestion, breathing, gland activity).

flashcard_questions.q: Which branch of the ANS activates the fight or flight response — sympathetic or parasympathetic?
Which branch of the ANS restores the body to a calm resting state after a threat?
Which hormone is released during the fight or flight response?
Name two physical changes the fight or flight response causes in the body.
flashcard_questions.a: Increased heart rate and blood redirected to the muscles.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the fight or flight response do to digestion?
flashcard_questions.a: Suppresses (slows or stops) it, as it is non-essential during a threat.

flashcard_questions.q: Who proposed the James–Lange theory of emotion and when?
flashcard_questions.a: William James and Carl Lange, independently in 1884.

flashcard_questions.q: According to the James–Lange theory, which comes first: the physical reaction or the emotion?
flashcard_questions.a: The physical reaction — the emotion follows as the brain's interpretation.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one strength of the James–Lange theory of emotion.
flashcard_questions.a: People with spinal cord injuries report reduced emotional intensity, supporting the role of physical feedback.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one weakness of the James–Lange theory of emotion.
flashcard_questions.a: Different emotions (e.g. fear and excitement) produce similar bodily states, so the body alone cannot distinguish them.

glossary_terms.definition: The body's rapid communication system, made up of the brain, spinal cord and all the nerves throughout the body.
The part of the nervous system consisting of the brain and spinal cord, which processes and integrates information.
All the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.
The division of the PNS that controls voluntary movements of the skeletal muscles and carries sensory information to the CNS.
The division of the PNS that controls involuntary bodily functions such as heart rate, digestion and breathing, and is split into sympathetic and parasympathetic branches.
The body's automatic response to a perceived threat, in which the sympathetic nervous system prepares the body to either confront or escape the danger.
The theory proposed by William James and Carl Lange that emotions are the result of our interpretation of bodily changes, not the cause of them.
